title: Impact of Merit Scholarships on College Enrollment

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Causal method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD).  
Why: The merit scholarship is assigned mechanically once a student’s GPA crosses a known cutoff. Treatment probability jumps from 0 to 1 at that point, fitting the classic sharp‐RDD set-up.  
Key assumptions:  
• Continuity – In the absence of the scholarship, the conditional expectation of college enrollment would be smooth in GPA at the cutoff (no other forces create a discrete jump).  
• No precise manipulation – Students cannot perfectly manipulate their GPA right around the threshold (validated with a density/McCrary test).  

## 2. R Code
```r
# --------------------------------------------
# Impact of Merit Scholarship on College Enrollment
# --------------------------------------------
# Load packages
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr)
  library(rdrobust)   # main RDD estimator
  library(rddensity)  # McCrary density test
})

# 1. Read the data
data_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s85_data.csv"
df <- read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Define the cutoff: 0.5 GPA (verified from treated indicator pattern)
cutoff <- 0.5

# 3. Main RDD estimate (local linear, MSE-optimal bandwidth)
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = df$y, x = df$running_var, c = cutoff)

cat("\n--- Main RDD estimate (local linear) ---\n")
cat("Treatment effect (taû) =", round(rd_main$coef[1], 4), 
    " | SE =", round(rd_main$se[1], 4), 
    " | p-value =", round(rd_main$pval[1], 4), "\n")

# 4. Robustness checks --------------------------------------------

## 4a. Bandwidth sensitivity (half & double the MSE-optimal bandwidth)
h_opt <- rd_main$bws[1,1]   # optimal bandwidth on left; use it symmetrically
rd_half <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, h = h_opt/2)
rd_double <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, h = h_opt*2)

cat("\n--- Bandwidth sensitivity ---\n")
cat("Half-bandwidth  taû =", round(rd_half$coef[1],4), 
    " | p =", round(rd_half$pval[1],4),"\n")
cat("Double-bandwidth taû =", round(rd_double$coef[1],4), 
    " | p =", round(rd_double$pval[1],4),"\n")

## 4b. Higher-order polynomial (quadratic)
rd_quad <- rdrobust(df$y, df$running_var, c = cutoff, p = 2)
cat("\n--- Polynomial order robustness (quadratic) ---\n")
cat("Quadratic taû =", round(rd_quad$coef[1],4), 
    " | p =", round(rd_quad$pval[1],4),"\n")

## 4c. Manipulation test (McCrary density)
dens_test <- rddensity(df$running_var, c = cutoff)
cat("\n--- McCrary density test ---\n")
cat("Log-density discontinuity =", round(dens_test$test$statistic,4), 
    " | p =", round(dens_test$test$p.value,4),"\n")
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Because a merit scholarship reduces the net cost of college, students just above the GPA cutoff should enroll at higher rates than those just below. I expect:  
• Sign: positive (τ > 0).  
• Magnitude: roughly +0.15 to +0.25 in enrollment probability (i.e., a 15–25 pp jump) given typical scholarship effects in the literature and the previewed spread in y values.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: The analysis exploits the GPA threshold as a cutoff to compare students just above and below the threshold.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Meeting the GPA threshold for a merit scholarship significantly increases college enrollment rates.
